sweep_summary: Cayubaba (cayu1262, isolate; catalog fixed-dominant antepenultimate, deciding source Key 1961:148-149 already held and verified). this search of works with stress in the title produced a single title hit, Hayes 1995 Metrical Stress Theory, which treats Cayuvava in section 8.2 as its canonical ternary-stress case. That section is not obtainable openly: no archive. ~88-124) contain only cross-references (Cayuvava = syllabic trochees, no monosyllables, non-persistent footing, top-down stressing of imperatives, all pointing to § 8.2), and Kager 1994 ROA-35 § 7.1 (held) reports Hayes's rule set (final extrametricality except in disyllables, right-to-left trochees under weak local parsing) with outputs dá.pa, tó.mo.ho, a.rí.po.ro, a.ri.pí.ri.to, á.ri.hi.hí.be.e.. - i.e. as reported it confirms the catalog rule. Hayes is a secondary re-analysis of Key's data, so it cannot supersede the deciding source; priority medium for a library pull of § 8.2 (check his statement of the imperative/lexical-stress exceptions). Best first-hand statement re-read this search of works with stress in the title is Key 1961 § 2.5.3 itself (quoted); no reclassification indicated.

new_statements.quote: There are two degrees of phonemic stress in Cayuvava, weak and strong. Strong stress generally occurs on the antepenultimate syllable of utterances of three or more syllables, and on the initial syllable of shorter utterances. [...] Certain imperative verb forms have strong stress on the final syllable [...] Strong stress occurs on the antepenultimate syllable and every third syllable preceding it. This appears to be a sentence-level pattern but it can be interrupted by any morpheme with phonemic strong stress. Thereafter the pattern will resume, counting from the interrupting strong-stressed morpheme.

new_statements.reading: First-hand fieldworker statement: strong (primary) stress on the antepenult of any utterance/stress group of three or more syllables, on the initial syllable of disyllables, with further strong stresses every third syllable leftward (ternary rhythm); exceptions are morphemes with their own lexical strong stress and final-stressed imperatives, and the counting domain is the utterance/stress group rather than the grammatical word. This is a dominant, not exceptionless, antepenultimate rule - consistent with the catalog's fixed-dominant coding and antepenultimate stress.

sources.quote: 'Cayuvava (Key 1961) has no contrast of syllable weight. Stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable and on every third syllable preceding it. However, disyllabic words are stressed on the penult. Each stress is reported to be equally strong.' Word-level forms (dá.pa, tó.mo.ho, a.rí.po.ro, a.ri.pí.ri.to, á.ri.hi.hí.be.e, ma.rá.ha.ha.é.i.ki, i.ki.tá.pa.re.ré.pe.ha ...). Secondary/theoretical; treats the pattern as word stress and notes Key reports no primary/secondary ranking among strong stresses, so the catalog's single '1' in 000100/0000100/00000100 is a convention, not Key's claim.
